Error bars indicate 95% confidence intervals. d. Power comparison between TransMap-local (y-axis) and TransPCO (x-axis) across matched simulation conditions. Colors indicate per-SNP trans heritability, shapes indicate the proportion of causal trans-eGene in each program, and interior marks indicate the residual correlation. The dashed line indicates equal power between two methods. e. Simulation design for global programs following the ARCHIE framework, with 20 additional cis-effect only variants. f. Recovered variant-gene effect matrices from ARCHIE and TransMap-global for one simulated replicate (top), and precision-recall curves for recovering true variant-gene pairs at three per-SNP trans heritability (bottom). Numerical results are reported in Supplementary Data.

Multi-scale trans-regulatory mapping reveals complementary disease genetic architectures

We next applied TransMap to bulk and single-nucleus RNA-sequencing profiles across 6 brain cell types and 3 brain cortical regions from the aging brain cortex in the ROSMAP cohort (average N = 481, Figure 2a, Supplementary Table 1, see Supplementary Figure 3a and Supplementary Notes S1-S2 for technical choices). Across cell types and contexts, we identified 17,054 significant TransMap-eGene QTL associations across 16,901 genes, 21,315 significant TransMap-local QTL associations across 6,453 Hotspot co-expression programs and 4,507 significant TransMap-global QTL associations across 2,700 global programs (FDR < 5%, Methods, Figure 2b). Among significant TransMap-eGene QTL associations, 19.9% involved genetic signals associated with multiple distal genes, compared with 10.5% of cis-eQTL associations involving multiple proximal genes. Similarly, 26.4% of TransMap-local QTL associations involved multiple programs. Given the large number of correlated molecular phenotypes and genome-wide genetic associations evaluated in trans-QTL mapping, we independently assessed the empirical calibration of the nominal FDR-controlled discoveries using genotypelabel permutations. The empirical FDR ranged 4.8%-9.2% in bulk contexts and ranged 7.7% to 14.9% across six cell types (Supplementary Figure 3b), indicating that conventional significance thresholds did not uniformly achieve nominal FDR control for single-phenotype trans-QTL mapping. These findings motivate the integration of complementary molecular-QTL evidence through multi-phenotype colocalization to provide additional statistical support for weak distal genetic associations, as evaluated in subsequent sections.

We generated 3 genome-wide variant-level trans-MaxPIP annotations separately for individual-gene (TransMap-eGene-MaxPIP), local-program (TransMap-local-MaxPIP) and global-program (TransMap-global-MaxPIP) phenotypes by aggregating fine-mapping posterior inclusion probabilities across phenotypes and cell types (Methods). We evaluated their disease relevance using two S-LDSC metrics: heritability enrichment and standardized effect size (𝜏 ⋆ ), the latter quantifying annotation informativeness conditional on other annotations in the model. In the meta-analysis across 57 traits, 2 out of 3 annotations (TransMap-eGene-MaxPIP and TransMap-local-MaxPIP) showed high heritability enrichment (2.75x-2.88x) (p-value ranging from 2.9 × 10 "23 to 4.3 × 10 "24 ) and 𝜏 ⋆ (0.22-0.27) (p-value ranging from 6.5 × 10 "56 to 3.5 × 10 "55 ) conditional on the baseline annotations (Figure 2c). Both annotations showed significant heritability enrichment and 𝜏 ⋆ when meta-analyzed across 18 brain-related traits and 22 blood-related traits, and remained significant when modeled jointly and consistent results were observed in brain-and blood-related trait meta-analyses (Figure 2c). These results indicate that individual distal genes and compact local programs capture complementary components of complex-trait genetic architecture, whereas broad global programs contribute no detectable heritability beyond baseline annotations.

We next benchmarked the disease relevance of TransMap annotations against existing approaches. At the local program scale, we compared TransMap-local-MaxPIP annotation against analogous trans-MaxPIP annotations generated using Eigengene, TransPCO and AUCell approaches (Methods). Because TransPCO combines multiple principal components (PC)-level association statistics using an ACAT omnibus test, we adapted it for fine-mapping by separately fine-mapping retained PCs and aggregating their PIPs into a MaxPIP annotation (TransPCO*-MaxPIP; Methods). TransMap-local-MaxPIP consistently exhibited 1.6x-3.0x higher heritability enrichment than the competing annotations across all-trait, blood-related and brain-related trait meta-analyses (Figure 2d, Supplementary Figure 4a). Both TransMap-local-MaxPIP and TransPCO*-MaxPIP showed significant heritability information (𝜏 ⋆ ) in meta-analyses across these trait categories. Notably, TransMap-local-MaxPIP exhibited 1.5x-2.3x higher 𝜏 ⋆ compared to TransPCO*-MaxPIP, and was the only annotation retaining significant positive conditional 𝜏 ⋆ when the two annotations were jointly included in the heritability model (Figure 2d, Supplementary Figure 4a). Besides the fine-mapping based comparison, we generated native TransPCO variant-level associations for 43,090 xQTL-informed independent variants (𝑟 7 <0.1, Supplementary Note S3), and compared heritability information against TransMap-local-MaxPIP restricted to these variants. TransMaplocal-MaxPIP retained its improved performance in this comparison (Supplementary Figure 4b). When WGCNA programs were used instead of Hotspot, TransMap-local-MaxPIP showed 13.9% lower heritability enrichment and 42.1% lower marginal 𝜏 ⋆ across the meta-analyses (Figure 2d, Supplementary Figure 4a). Nevertheless, WPC-based TransMap-local annotations remained more disease-informative than competing program-level approaches when applied to the same WGCNA programs, indicating that the advantage of background-whitened program representations is not restricted to Hotspot-derived programs. At global program scale, we benchmarked TransMap-global against ARCHIE 17 . Neither TransMap-global-MaxPIP or ARCHIE-MaxPIP showed significant heritability signals across all three meta-analyses (Supplementary Figure 4c). Therefore, we restricted all downstream program analyses to local Hotspot programs. At individual gene scale, TransMap-eGene-MaxPIP annotation showed 1.95x higher 𝜏 ⋆ in all traits meta-analysis compared to fine-mapping centered around significant trans-eQTL at FDR<5% as performed in eQTLGen Phase II 9 , while marginally associated trans-eQTL (p-value< 10 "0 ) did not show a significant 𝜏 ⋆ (Supplementary Figure 4d). In a joint S-LDSC model, TransMap-eGene-MaxPIP remained the only annotation with a significant positive 𝜏 ⋆ (𝜏 ⋆ =0.35, p-value=6.6 × 10 "88 ) (Supplementary Figure 4d). Thus, retaining genome-wide fine-mapping posterior evidence captured distributed disease-relevant trans-regulatory information that was lost when downstream analyses were restricted to conventionally significant trans-eQTL; suggesting hidden heritability information.

We compared the proportion of trait heritability captured by cis-MaxPIP annotations, defined as the maximum fine-mapping PIP for each variant across cis-eGenes and cell types 25 , with that captured by individual-gene (TransMap-eGene-MaxPIP) and local-program (TransMap-local-MaxPIP) trans-QTL annotations. Across 28 brain-related traits 26, 41 (Supplementary Table 4), individual-gene trans-MaxPIP annotations captured a greater proportion of heritability than cis-MaxPIP annotations for 9 of 28 traits. When individual-gene and local-program trans annotations were combined, this increased to 26 of 28 traits (Figure 2e; Supplementary Figure 4e), highlighting the additional disease-heritability information captured when local-program annotations are combined with individual-gene trans-QTL annotations. This pattern was particularly pronounced for Autism and Schizophrenia, whereas AD and multiple sclerosis showed more comparable proportions of heritability captured by cis-and trans-MaxPIP annotations.

We performed two secondary analyses. First, we assessed whether TransMap yielded reproducible variant-level trans-MaxPIP annotations across independent datasets. For each expression profile, we randomly split donors 50:50, independently reconstructed the three scales of trans phenotypes, and repeated genome-wide finemapping in both donor subsets (Methods). The resulting split-level trans-MaxPIP annotations showed Pearson's correlations ranging from 0.45 to 0.79 across regulatory scales (Supplementary Figure 5a). Despite the reduced sample sizes, the individual-gene and local-program annotations showed consistent disease-heritability signals, with significant enrichment and positive marginal 𝜏 * estimates in both splits (Supplementary Figure 5b). Second, we evaluated whether the framework could extend beyond data-derived local co-expression programs to two prespecified functional classes: 50 curated MSigDB Hallmark gene sets 16, 42, 43 and cell-type-resolved SCENIC regulons 44 (Methods). WPC-derived TransMap annotations from both program classes showed stronger disease-heritability informativeness than competing program-scoring approaches (Supplementary Figures 5c-d). When jointly modeled with our primary individual-gene and local-program TransMap annotations, most of their disease-relevant information was explained away, although Hallmark annotations retained additional conditional informativeness for blood-related traits (Supplementary Figure 5e).

We conclude that genome-wide trans-QTL fine-mapping yields reproducible and disease-informative variant annotations, with individual distal genes and compact local programs capturing complementary components of complex-trait genetic architecture.

Trans-regulatory loci from TransMap colocalize with proximal gene regulation and downstream biomarker-QTL and exhibit distinct functional architectures

Having established the disease relevance of individual-gene and local-program trans-QTL annotations, we next investigated whether distal genetic associations could be linked to proximal gene regulation and downstream bulk-level biomarker molecular phenotypes (proteins, glycoproteins and metabolites) through shared genetic signals. We performed a genome-wide multi-phenotype colocalization using ColocBoost 25 (Methods), representing each shared causal variant by a colocalization confidence set (CoS) if it contained at least one variant at p-value<10 "0 and its associated configuration of molecular phenotypes sharing the genetic signal. Across the genome, we retained 49,532 colocalization events involving trans-eGenes or trans-ePrograms with support from at least one proximal cis-eQTL or additional biomarker-QTL (Figure 3a, Supplementary Figure 6a). To assess the empirical reliability of these shared-signal associations, we performed two complementary permutation analyses, yielding empirical FDR estimates of 0.4%-1.34% for genome-wide trans-phenotype colocalization and 0.52%-0.95% for matched cis-trans configurations (Methods, Supplementary Figure 3b). When evaluated against independent cell-type resolved trans-eQTL maps in PsychAD 13 (N=1,494 samples), Colocalization-supported trans-eQTL associations showed 11.1-to 21.9-fold higher recall across cell types for similar precision compared to fine-mapped trans-eQTL hits (Figure 3b). Colocalization-supported trans-eQTL associations aggregated across cell types also showed higher recall with respect to the MetaBrain bulk trans-eQTL 10 (N=2,683 samples) compared to fine-mapped trans-eQTL hits (Supplementary Figure 6b). The lower empirical FDR estimates and stronger external concordance support the increased reliability of colocalizationsupported distal genetic associations compared to standard single-phenotype trans-QTL maps. Among all cis-eQTL signals, 26.7% were linked to at least one distal trans-regulatory phenotype, including 17.3% linked to both individual-gene and program-level trans phenotypes (Supplementary Figure 6c), revealing shared genetic associations across distinct scales of distal expression regulation.

We designated colocalization events containing at least one cis-eGene and one trans-eGene or trans-eProgram as candidate cis-trans regulatory configurations (Methods). These included 2,198 cis-trans configurations and 1,825 cis-trans-biomarker configurations. We next examined whether program-level trans-QTL showed stronger genetic convergence with biomarker-QTL than individual-gene trans-QTL. Among trans-QTL loci with biomarker-QTL support, 86.4% were connected to individual trans-eGenes and 59.6% to trans-ePrograms, with substantial overlap of 46.2% across two trans-regulatory scales (Supplementary Figure 6d). Despite their lower representation among biomarker-supported loci, trans-eProgram QTL showed 1.35-1.40-fold enrichment for biomarker-QTL convergence compared to trans-eGene QTL (Figure 3c), indicating that program-level phenotypes preferentially identify trans-regulatory effects with measurable downstream molecular consequences. Trans-eGene and trans-eProgram QTL identified in glial cell types showed stronger enrichment (1.27x-1.41x, p-value < 10 "0 ), whereas excitatory-neuron trans-QTL showed no significant enrichment across the three biomarker modalities (p-value=0.15; Supplementary Figure 6e).

We next examined the functional properties of genes associated with these colocalization events. We classified the colocalization events as cis-only, cis-trans or trans-only based on the representation of cis and trans phenotypes among colocalized phenotypes (Methods). Pairs of distal trans-eGenes implicated by the same colocalization event showed 1.5-fold enrichment (p-value=0.009) for known protein-protein interactions in the STRING database 45 , whereas pairs connecting proximal cis-eGenes and distal trans-eGenes showed no detectable enrichment (Figure 3f). Importantly, pairs of highly weighted genes within the same program exhibited an even higher 1.86-fold enrichment in protein-protein interactions. These results indicate that program-level trans-QTL preferentially implicate groups of functionally connected genes, complementing their stronger convergence with biomarker-QTL. We further examined whether cis-only, cis-trans and trans-only colocalization events exhibited distinct genomic and evolutionary properties. Genes nearest to trans-only QTL were significantly enriched for a curated set of 1,639 human transcription factors 46 (1.2x-1.3x with p-value < 0.001) (Supplementary Figure 7a). Cis-only and cis-trans variants were located closer to transcription start sites and showed stronger evolutionary conservation 47, 48 than trans-only variants (Supplementary Figures 7b-c). However, genes nearest to trans-only loci showed greater enrichment for loss-of-function constraint, with 1.64fold and 1.58-fold enrichment for loci involving trans-eGenes and trans-ePrograms, respectively (p-value < 0.001; Supplementary Figure 7d). These findings reveal distinct patterns of evolutionary constraint at transonly loci, with weaker variant-level conservation but greater loss-of-function intolerance among nearby genes.

This observation is consistent with recent reports that trans-regulatory loci can occur near highly constrained genes 46 , although the functional relationship between these genes and the associated distal molecular phenotypes remains unresolved.

Overall, these analyses establish that multi-phenotype colocalization provides additional statistical support for distal genetic associations and reveals complementary molecular and functional properties of individual-gene and program-level trans-QTL. In particular, local-program associations show stronger convergence with biomarker variation and functionally connected gene networks, supporting their utility for interpreting distal regulatory effects across molecular layers.

Neuronal cis effects converge on coordinated glial trans responses

Having identified candidate cis-trans regulatory configurations, we next investigated whether shared genetic signals revealed systematic relationships between proximal and distal regulatory effects across brain cell types. Out of 4,023 cis-trans colocalization events, 32.3% involved distinct initiating and recipient cell types (Figure 4a). Trans-QTL represented in these colocalization events showed greater cell type specificity compared to cis-eQTL (Figure 4a). Cis-eQTL were distributed similarly between neuronal and glial populations, whereas trans-QTLs were enriched in glial cell types and relatively depleted in neurons (Figure 4b, Supplementary Figure 8a). Permutation tests revealed significant enrichment of neuronal-initiated, glial-recipient configurations among the initiating and recipient cell type pairs underlying the colocalization events (Methods, FDR<5%; Figure 4c, Supplementary Figure 8b). Conversely, excitatory neurons showed depleted representations among recipient cell types (0.34x-0.86x), with the strongest depletion observed for inhibitory-neuron-initiated configurations (Figure 4d, Supplementary Figure 8c). A similar pattern was observed when trans-eGene and trans-eProgram QTL were considered separately, supporting consistency across regulatory scales (Supplementary Figures 8d-e). We assessed whether these patterns could be explained by differences in cell-type representation as excitatory neurons comprised a large 39.8% of the 630K cells studied. We therefore performed donor-stratified subsampling of excitatory neurons, independently reconstructing their cis-and trans-eQTL maps while leaving other cell types unchanged (Methods). Enrichment of excitatory-neuron-initiated, glial-recipient configurations and the greater representation of excitatory neurons among initiating cell types persisted across the subsampled datasets (Supplementary Figures 8f-g). Fewer than 0.5% of the candidate cis-trans configurations overlapped detectable cell type fraction QTL, suggesting that the observed asymmetry was not predominantly explained by the cell-composition QTL identified in this cohort (Supplementary Figure 8h-i).

We next evaluated whether neuronal-initiated, glial-recipient configurations were associated with coherent biological pathways and molecular functions. Among colocalization events involving excitatory neuron cis effects, astrocyte recipient trans-eGenes were enriched for asparagine N-linked glycosylation and post-translational protein modification (FDR<5%; Figure 4e). We additionally identified 26 colocalization events involving 53 glycoproteins, with enrichment for Neurofascin-and L1CAM-related interaction pathways, involving genes such as NRCAM, CNTNAP1 and NFASC (FDR<5%, Supplementary Figure 9a). Of these glycoproteins, 52.5% showed STRING protein-protein interaction connections with colocalized astrocyte trans-eGenes (score>0.4 45 ; Supplementary Figure 9b). Microglial trans-eGenes linked to excitatory-neuron cis effects were strongly enriched for RHO-ROCK signaling and a SEMA4D-associated cell-migration pathway (FDR<5%, Figure 4e). These pathways shared genes including RHOB, ROCK2, LIMK1 and MYL12B, consistent with previously reported roles of Rho-family signaling and SEMA4D in microglial responses 49, 50 . These findings indicate that candidate cross-cell-type configurations implicate distinct, functionally coherent glial programs associated with proximal neuronal genetic signals.

We next sought orthogonal support for the inferred neuronal-glial configurations using independent neuronastrocyte co-culture transcriptomic data and spatial transcriptomic measurements from the ROSMAP cortex. First, in the co-culture experiment, human Ngn2-induced excitatory neurons were cultured with and without mouse cortical astrocytes and profiled by single-cell RNA sequencing at five time points 51 . Differentially expressed genes were pooled across time points for downstream enrichment analyses (Methods, Figure 4f). Excitatory-neuron trans-eGenes from astrocyte-initiated configurations were specifically 1.43-fold enriched among neuronal genes responsive to astrocyte co-culture (Figure 4f). Similarly, astrocyte trans-eGenes from excitatory-neuron-initiated configurations were 1.32-fold enriched among astrocytic genes responsive to neuronal co-culture. This directional correspondence was observed for both trans-eGenes and key driver genes of trans-ePrograms (Supplementary Figure 9c). Second, we examined the anatomical organization of neuronal-glial configurations using 10x Visium spatial transcriptomic data from 32 ROSMAP cortical tissue sections spanning different stages of AD pathology 52 (Methods, Figure 4g). Cis-regulated neuronal genes participating in neuronal-glial configurations showed preferential expression in deep cortical layers (L4-L6) proximal to the white matter compared to the outer layers (L1-L3), whereas their associated glial trans-regulated genes were enriched in adjacent white matter regions (Methods, Figure 4g, Supplementary Figure 9d). The pattern was preserved across pathological stages and across strata of amyloid-plaque burden (Supplementary Figure 9e). Although spot-level resolution precludes direct inference of cell-cell contact, these results place candidate initiating neuronal genes and recipient glial responses in anatomically adjacent cortical compartments. To illustrate how TransMap resolves candidate cross-cell-type regulatory configurations at individual genetic loci, we first examined an excitatory neuron-initiated (cis) and microglial-recipient (trans) colocalization event in the SEC61G gene locus (CoS spanning chr7:54723624-54780677). The SEC61G cis-eQTL in excitatory neurons colocalized with 23 microglial trans-eGene QTL, as well as 2 microglial trans-eProgram QTL (Program 31 and Program 100) (Figure 5a). To investigate whether variation in neuronal SEC61G expression statistically mediated the corresponding microglial trans associations, we applied structural equation model 53 (SEM) separately for each colocalized microglial trans-eGene and trans-eProgram (Methods). 10 gene-level and 2 program-level associations showed significant indirect effects (p-value < 0.05 based on donor bootstrap analysis) (Figures 5b). Both colocalized trans-ePrograms also contained multiple genes with marginal associations at this locus: 2 of 49 genes in Program 31 and 2 of 18 in Program 100 had p-value< 10 "0 . Pathway analysis linked Program 31 to the TYROBP causal network in microglia (FDR=0.006) and erythropoietin-activated PI3K signaling (FDR=0.01; Figure 5c), whereas Program 100 was enriched for nephrin-family interactions (FDR=0.0034) and RHO GTPase-related pathways (FDR=0.004; Supplementary Figure 10a). To investigate the anatomical distribution of the genes implicated by this candidate configuration, we examined SEC61G and the associated microglial trans-gene MAP4K4 in ROSMAP Visium spatial transcriptomic sections spanning different stages of AD pathology. SEC61G expression was more prominent across cortical layers, whereas MAP4K4 expression was stronger in white-matter regions (Figure 5d), consistent with the broader spatial organization observed for neuronal cis-and glial trans-associated genes (Figure 4g). We next examined a complementary configuration linking neuronal cis regulation to astrocytic transcriptional programs and glycoprotein variation. Consistent with the enrichment of astrocytic trans-eGenes for N-linked glycosylation pathways, an excitatory-neuron GDA cis-eQTL (CoS spanning chr9:72,219,468-72,236,972) colocalized with QTL for 9 glycoproteins, including NRCAM, CNTNAP1, NFASC and CNTN2, and a 97-gene astrocytic trans-eProgram (Supplementary Figure 10b). These 9 glycoproteins were consistently enriched for neurofascin interactions and L1CAM interactions with FDR < 0.01 (Supplementary Figure 10c). The astrocytic trans-eProgram was included heavily prioritized genes SLC3A2, ALG3, KDELR1 and SEC24C, that overlapped genes responsive to neuron-responsive astrocyte genes in the co-culture experiment (Supplementary Figure 10d). Although SEM found no significant indirect association through GDA excitatory neuron expression or astrocyte trans-eProgram to glycoproteins, the STRING protein-protein interaction network linked the glycoproteins to genes in astrocyte trans-eProgram (Supplementary Figure 10e).

These analyses reveal an asymmetric organization of cell-type-resolved cis-trans genetic associations, characterized by preferential convergence of proximal neuronal signals with functionally coherent glial distal responses. Concordance with co-culture transcriptional responses and spatial organization provides complementary biological support for these candidate cross-cell-type regulatory configurations.

Multiscale trans-regulatory maps resolve the functional architecture of Alzheimer's disease loci

We evaluated how TransMap trans-QTL resolve the regulatory architecture of Alzheimer's disease. We performed AD-centered multi-phenotype colocalization analysis integrating cis-eGene, trans-eGene, trans-eProgram and biomarker-QTL maps with a recent AD GWAS meta-analysis 54 (cases=128,681, controls=849,833) (Methods). Overall, we identified 118 colocalization events involving AD and at least one molecular-QTL (Figure 6a). For 51.7% of these events, the corresponding AD GWAS locus lacked a wellresolved 95% credible set from GWAS-only SuSiE fine-mapping, illustrating how molecular-QTL integration can nominate shared regulatory signals at loci that remain poorly resolved by GWAS fine-mapping alone. (Supplementary Figure 11a). 84 of these 118 colocalization events showed both cis-and trans-QTL evidence, 3 showed cis-only evidence and 31 showed trans-only evidence; 70.4% of the events involving trans-QTL had support across multiple trans-regulatory layers. Trans-eProgram QTL showed 1.43-fold enrichment among AD colocalization events relative to trans-eGene QTL (p-value= 5.4 × 10 "27 ; Figure 6b). Among AD colocalization events involving trans-eGene QTL and trans-eProgram QTL, 74.8% also showed biomarker-QTL evidence (Figure 6a), revealing frequent convergence of disease association signals with distal expression phenotypes and additional molecular traits. No AD-molecular-QTL colocalization events were recovered under the genotypepermutation null, providing additional empirical support for the observed associations (Methods). These results highlight the utility of trans regulatory information specifically in the context of understanding AD disease genetics. Bulk tissue cis-eQTL were more frequently represented among AD colocalization events than bulk tissue trans-QTL (20.7% versus 4.3%; Supplementary Figure 11b). AD colocalization events frequently involved distinct trans phenotypes across multiple cellular contexts; 59 loci implicated more than three recipient cell types (Figure 6b). This extends prior observations that a single AD locus may engage distinct distal genes or programs across several brain cell populations 55 . Microglia was the most frequently represented initiating cell types, and astrocytes and OPC were significantly enriched among recipient cell types (Supplementary Figures 11c-d).

We next investigated whether AD-colocalized variants exhibited distinct evolutionary properties according to their molecular-QTL configurations. For each AD-cis, AD-trans or combined AD-cis-trans colocalization event, we selected the variant with the highest variant colocalization probability (VCP) and compared its evolutionary conservation score 47, 48 (Methods). Variants supported by both cis-and trans-QTL colocalization showed the highest conservation scores, significantly exceeding those with trans-only support (p-value = 0.0007; Figure 6c). As a GWAS-only reference, we selected the highest-PIP variant from AD fine-mapping at loci without detectable cis-or trans-QTL colocalization. These AD-only variants also showed significantly greater conservation than ADtrans-only variants (p-value = 0.04; Figure 6c). To explore whether variant conservation differed across cellular configurations, we regressed conservation scores against indicators of candidate initiating cell types, recipient cell types and initiating-recipient pairs (Methods). No initiating cell type was significantly associated with greater conservation. Among recipient cell types, microglia and oligodendrocytes were associated with higher conservation (p-value = 0.01 for each), whereas astrocytes and inhibitory neurons were associated with lower conservation (p-value = 0.02 for each; Supplementary Figure 11e). Exploratory pair-level analyses also identified nominally higher conservation for selected excitatory-neuron-initiated configurations involving OPC, oligodendrocyte and microglial recipient phenotypes (Supplementary Figure 11e). These findings suggest that evolutionary conservation varies across AD-associated molecular QTL configurations and their implicated cell types, complementing the neuronal-glial asymmetry observed genome-wide.

We visualized the genome-wide distribution of AD-associated molecular-QTL evidence by annotating the AD GWAS Manhattan plot with colocalized cis-and trans-regulatory phenotypes (Figure 6d; Supplementary Figure 11f). This revealed substantial heterogeneity in the regulatory evidence associated with different AD loci. Some loci were predominantly supported by multiple distal regulatory phenotypes, including the APP region (highest VCP variant rs432766), whereas others showed convergence of proximal and distal associations, such as the BIN1 locus (rs6733839), linking BIN1 cis-eQTL with an AP4M1 trans-eQTL, and the APH1B locus (rs117618017), linking APH1B cis-eQTL with 11 trans-eGenes, including IKBKE, and two trans-ePrograms. Several loci with comparatively modest AD association statistics also showed colocalization with multiple distal or biomarker phenotypes, illustrating the additional molecular context provided by integrated genetic associations. To assess the reproducibility of these findings across AD genetic studies, we repeated AD-focused TransMap colocalization using a previous GWAS meta-analysis 56 with a smaller effective sample size (111,326 cases and 677,663 controls). This analysis replicated 69 out of the 118 colocalization events, including 44 with replicated cis-and trans-QTL evidence (Supplementary Figure 12).

These analyses demonstrate how multiscale, cell-type-resolved trans-QTL maps enhance the discovery and functional characterization of AD-associated regulatory signals by prioritizing candidate regulatory genes, coordinated expression programs, cellular contexts and biomarker-associated molecular phenotypes at AD susceptibility loci.

Multiscale cis-trans regulatory maps connect genes across independent AD susceptibility loci

We next examined two case studies illustrating how multiscale trans-regulatory mapping can connect molecular associations across independent AD susceptibility loci and nominate candidates for experimental follow-up.

We first examined an AD-associated locus near KNOP1 on chromosome 16 57, 58 , where an astrocytic KNOP1 cis-eQTL colocalized with a microglial trans-eProgram (Program 27) containing MS4A4E, MS4A6A, APOE and RIN3 (Figure 7a). Among the distal molecular phenotypes implicated at this locus, microglial Program 27 showed the strongest statistical support for an indirect association in SEM analysis (Supplementary Figure 13a). Astrocytic KNOP1 expression exhibited the largest estimated indirect effect among the evaluated proximal candidates (Figure 7b). The 87-gene Program 27 included MS4A4E, which ranked fourth among constituent genes by marginal trans-association significance, and STRING analysis placed MS4A4E in a functionally connected component with APOE, RIN3 and MS4A6A (Figure 7c). Interestingly, MS4A4E was also implicated as a proximal cis-regulated gene at the independent chromosome 11 MS4A-family AD locus 59 . AD-centered colocalization at this locus identified 2 distinct colocalization confidence sets with different molecular-QTL configurations (minimum between-set purity = 0.44; Figure 7d), consistent with distinct signals also identified by AD GWAS fine-mapping. One colocalization event included microglia-specific cis-effects at MS4A4A and MS4A6A, the other one included MS4A4E cis-eQTL in DLPFC and 9 trans-eGene-QTLs and 3 trans-eProgram-QTL in inhibitory neurons (52.2% of all colocalized trans phenotypes; Supplementary Figure 13b). STRING protein-protein interaction analysis revealed functional connections among the implicated inhibitory-neuron trans-eGenes and colocalized protein phenotypes (Supplementary Figure 13c). One of the colocalized trans-ePrograms (program 59) was enriched in MECP2-related transcription and protein-folding pathways, (FDR < 5%; Supplementary Figures 13d-e). These observations connect two independent AD susceptibility loci through MS4A4E, which appears as a distal member of a microglial program associated with the KNOP1 locus and as a proximal cis-regulated gene at the MS4A locus, where the same genetic signal also implicates an inhibitory-neuron program enriched for MECP2-related transcription 60, 61 . This cross-locus convergence implicated by TransMap nominates MS4A4E for AD susceptibility, but whether it play the key role of AD risk at MS4A-family locus remains to be established experimentally.

We next examined a complementary cross-locus configuration beginning with INO80E at the chromosome 16p11.2 BP4-BP5 region 62, 63 , a structurally complex genomic locus. At this locus, an AD-associated signal colocalized with cis-eQTL for ten genes across expression contexts and a DLPFC trans-eQTL for ABCA1, an established AD-associated gene at an independent chromosome 9 locus 64, 65 (Figure 7e; Supplementary Table 7). To prioritize candidate proximal regulators of the distal ABCA1 association, we fitted structural equation models with ABCA1 expression as the distal outcome (Methods). Among the ten proximal cis-eGenes, INO80E expression in excitatory neurons and oligodendrocytes showed nominally significant indirect associations with distal ABCA1 expression (p-value < 0.05; Figure 7f). INO80E encodes a subunit of the INO80 chromatin remodeling complex 66, 67 and belonged to a functionally connected group of these local cis-eGenes in the STRING network, while they did not connect with ABCA1 (Supplementary Figure 14a). We then examined indirect associations among the local cis-eGenes with INO80E by fitting additional mediations with INO80E alternately as mediator and outcome. These models yielded 14 and 15 indirect associations, respectively (p-value < 0.05; Supplementary Figures 14b-c). With INO80E modeled as the mediator, MAPK3 and KCTD13 showed the strongest indirect effects among the local genes. Although ERK1/2 and RhoA signaling have been implicated in ABCA1 regulation in other systems [68] [69] [70] [71] , whether INO80E contributes to the distal ABCA1 association through either gene remains to be tested experimentally. At the independent chromosome 9 ABCA1 locus, ABCA1 instead appeared as a proximal cis-regulated gene, with bulk-tissue ABCA1 cis-eQTL colocalizing with astrocytic and microglial trans-eProgram QTL (Figure 7g). These configurations also showed nominal support for indirect associations in SEM analyses. Within the 79-gene microglial program, FDFT1 ranked sixth by marginal transassociation significance and was functionally connected to ABCA1 in the STRING interaction network (Figure 7h). These results link independent AD-associated loci through ABCA1, which appears as a distal transregulated gene associated with the INO80E locus and as a proximal cis-regulated gene connected to glial regulatory programs at its own locus.

Discussion

TransMap provides a generalizable framework for performing (i) multiscale cell-type-resolved trans-QTL mapping, involving individual genes and gene programs, and (ii) multi-phenotype colocalization of these trans-QTL with cell-type-resolved cis-eQTL and biomarker-QTL. Applied to the aging human brain through the ADSP Functional Genomics Consortium (FunGen-AD), TransMap provides a cell-type-resolved atlas of transregulatory variation and their relationships with AD-associated genetic variation. The resulting maps reveal (i) complementary contributions of individual-gene and local program-level QTL annotations to complex trait heritability, (ii) stronger correspondence of program-level genetic signals with downstream biomarker-QTL and functional networks, (iii) candidate cis-trans regulatory configurations spanning distinct brain cell types, and (iv) expanded interpretation of AD susceptibility loci through shared genetic associations with distal genes, regulatory programs and molecular biomarkers.

A central insight from TransMap is that distal genetic regulation can be more sensitively detected and functionally characterized through coordinated molecular responses than through individual gene associations alone. Although a regulatory variant may exert only weak effects on individual distal genes, its effects can converge on groups of co-regulated genes, producing a more detectable program-level genetic signal. TransMap's whitened PCA approach improves the detection of coordinated trans effects while accounting for background expression covariance and capturing multiple axes of regulatory variation within a program. Notably, individual-gene and local-program trans-QTL annotations capture complementary components of complex-trait heritability despite being derived from the same transcriptomic measurements, highlighting the value of representing distal genetic regulation at multiple molecular scales. Complementing this program-based strategy, multi-phenotype colocalization leverages shared genetic signals across molecular phenotypes to support weak trans associations that may not achieve conventional significance thresholds individually. More broadly, the integration of multiple molecular modalities provides complementary views of the consequences of genetic variation, allowing evidence from proximal gene regulation, distal expression programs and molecular biomarkers to jointly inform transregulatory inference. By connecting these complementary molecular phenotypes through shared genetic signals, TransMap can pinpoint candidate regulatory relationships underlying an association, providing a more detailed basis for downstream functional investigation. The stronger convergence of program-level trans-QTL with biomarker-QTL and functional protein networks further suggests that coordinated expression programs provide informative representations of distal genetic effects across molecular layers. Moreover, the enrichment of neuronal cis-regulatory signals among loci associated with glial trans-regulatory responses, supported by coculture and spatial transcriptomic analyses, suggests that distal genetic regulation may involve relationships across cellular contexts rather than being restricted to the cell type containing the proximal genetic effect. This has broader implications for disease-variant interpretation, as the cellular context of proximal gene regulation may differ from those exhibiting associated distal molecular responses, as also highlighted in recent mouse models 72, 73 . These findings support a multiscale and multimodal view of trans regulation in which genetic effects are distributed across coordinated molecular programs, molecular layers and cellular contexts.

TransMap provides several reusable outputs and opportunities for downstream applications in human genetics. First, its modular end-to-end pipeline for trans-acting phenotype construction, genome-wide QTL fine-mapping, and multi-phenotype colocalization, can be deployed across diverse tissues, cell types and molecular QTL cohorts. This framework may be particularly useful in tissue-specific or cell-type-resolved QTL datasets with modest sample sizes, where conventional individual-gene trans-QTL discovery remains underpowered. Moreover, as molecular QTL resources expand across transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic and other molecular measurements, integrating these complementary genetic views offers opportunities to improve the detection and functional interpretation of distal regulatory effects. Second, although the gene programs examined in this study were primarily derived from the analyzed tissues, TransMap can also incorporate externally defined gene programs, including those identified from mouse models or genetic perturbation experiments, to investigate their regulation by human genetic variation. Third, genome-wide fine-mapped trans-eGene and trans-eProgram QTL provide variant-level annotations that can complement cis-eQTL annotations in functional annotation-based heritability analyses 32, 34 and potentially inform polygenic risk prediction 74, 75 and polygenic localization methods 30 across a broad range of complex diseases and traits. Fourth, cis-regulated genes and distal trans-eGenes or trans-ePrograms implicated through colocalization with disease GWAS provide specific molecular and cellular hypotheses for targeted functional validation. In particular, cell-type-resolved cis-trans regulatory configurations can guide the design of cell-type-specific CRISPR perturbation experiments in co-culture systems, where candidate cis-regulated genes are perturbed in putative initiating cell types and their predicted distal transcriptional responses are measured in recipient cell types 76 . Finally, while the present study primarily focuses on molecular assays with single readouts, we are currently extending TransMap to 10X scRNA+ATAC multiome datasets as part of the FunGen-AD effort to characterize distal genetic regulation across coupled molecular layers.

Our work has several limitations, representing important directions for future research. First, the substantial differences in effect sizes between proximal cis-eQTL and weaker distal trans-QTL create statistical challenges for performing untargeted multi-phenotype colocalization jointly across cis and trans phenotypes, motivating our strategy of performing separate cis-and trans-QTL colocalization analyses, followed by integration of colocalization events sharing genetic signals. Additionally, weak individual-gene cell-type-resolved trans-QTL associations exhibited elevated empirical false discovery rates despite nominal FDR control. In contrast, multiphenotype colocalization yielded trans-regulatory associations with lower empirical false discovery rates in the evaluated permutation analyses and stronger concordance with independent trans-QTL resources (Supplementary Figure 4c). Further methodological development is needed to accommodate differences in statistical power across molecular phenotypes and enable more comprehensive joint cis-trans colocalization. Second, although TransMap identifies candidate configurations through multi-phenotype colocalization, shared genetic associations do not establish that a cis-regulated gene causally mediates a downstream trans effect or that cross-cell-type associations reflect direct intercellular signaling. Although statistical mediation, co-culture and spatial transcriptomic analyses provide complementary support for selected configurations, targeted genetic perturbation experiments will be important for establishing the causal architecture of these regulatory relationships. Third, the performance of background-whitened PCA depends on accurately estimating the background expression covariance structure. Limited sample sizes, expression sparsity and heterogeneous cellular states may compromise this estimation and affect the sensitivity and interpretability of derived programs. Fourth, strong residual correlations among molecular phenotypes can result in loss of power for large-scale multiphenotype colocalization, as highlighted in the ColocBoost paper 25 . The residual correlations estimated in the present datasets fall within the range where statistical power and false discovery rates were generally well maintained 25 , and empirical permutation analyses further support favorable null calibration in the current application. Fifth, the present study does not systematically address cross-cohort harmonization of expression measurements, program definitions and genetic association signals, which will be necessary for integrating independently generated trans-QTL maps and improving portability across datasets and populations.

Methods

TransMap: an end-to-end framework for distal genetic regulation across cell types

TransMap is proposed as an end-to-end computational framework that represents trans regulation at three molecular resolutions from gene expression, including individual distal genes (trans-eGene) and gene programs (trans-eProgram). A gene program may be represented by a set of small number of genes (typically ranging from tens to hundreds of genes) or a continuous weighting of all genes genome-wide (Figure 1a). Each trans-acting gene or gene program within a cell type is encoded as a donor-level quantitative activity phenotype and carried through genome-wide LD-aware trans-QTL fine-mapping. These cell-type resolved trans-QTL are then analyzed together with cell-type-resolved cis-eQTL and downstream bulk tissue biomarker-QTL using multi-phenotype colocalization, which tests whether proximal cis signals, distal trans signals and downstream biomarker signals are consistent with a shared underlying genetic locus. Colocalization indicates compatibility with a shared causal variant across a set of molecular phenotypes but does not establish mediation or direct intercellular signaling. TransMap nominated candidate regulatory configurations represented by (cis-eGene, cis-effect cell type, trans-eGene/eProgram, trans-effect cell type, trans-biomarker). We term the cis-effect cell types as 'initiating cell types' and the distal trans-effect cell types as 'recipient cell types'. This design allows TransMap to compare regulatory evidence across scales and cell types for biological characterization.

Construction of multi-scale, cell-type-resolved trans-acting phenotypes

TransMap constructs cell-type-resolved, donor-level trans-acting molecular phenotypes from gene expression data at three resolutions: i) individual distal genes provide the most specific measured targets (TransMap-eGene), ii) local programs extract co-regulatory axes from compact co-expression neighborhoods (TransMaplocal), and iii) global programs capture broader axes of genetically coordinated expression learned from genomewide trans-association architecture (TransMap-global).

TransMap-eGene.

Let 𝑬 ∈ ℝ ,×/ denote the donor-level pseudo-bulk whole-genome mean-centered expression matrix for 𝑞 genes of 𝑛 individuals in each cell type or bulk context, after removal of relevance covariates considered in trans-eQTL analysis 10 (see Data resources and preprocessing below). Let 𝒀 𝒏 ×𝟏 𝒈 denote the standardized gene-expression vector across 𝑛 donors for gene 𝑔. These phenotypes represent the conventional unit of trans-eQTL mapping and provide the single-gene baseline for program-level analyses.

TransMap-local. TransMap-local converts compact co-expression genes into donor-level program activity phenotypes through two steps: (i) co-expression program detection and (ii) the program-level activity characterization across donors.

To detect compact co-expression modules in each cell type or bulk context, we implement Hotspot 28 on the expression matrix 𝑬, with donor similarity defined from the entire expression space. Gene modules were identified based on gene-level local autocorrelation on this donor-neighborhood graph (n_neighbors=30) and graph-smoothed local correlations among informative genes 28 . We considered minimum module-size thresholds of 10, 30, and 50 genes to evaluate local program definitions across module granularity, from fine-grained co-expression substructures to broader co-expression genes (Supplementary Note S4.1).

We first create 22 leave-one-chromosome-out (LOCO) programs, 𝒢 = "# , by leaving out all genes from chromosome 𝑐. Let 𝑬 = "# ∈ ℝ ,×/ ' "# denote the donor-by-gene expression matrix for program 𝑚, where 𝑞 = "# is the number of genes outside chromosome 𝑐. TransMap-local extracts donor-level co-regulatory activity from 𝑬 = "# using the whitened principal component (WPC) approach 23 . Let 𝚺 K = "# be the program-level covariance matrix for 𝒢 = "# ,, and 𝚺 *= "# be the background residual covariance matrix matched with 𝒢 = "# . WPC estimates loading directions by maximizing module variance contrastive to the background, which maximizes signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)

To avoid double usage of trans association evidence and ensure genuine trans effects, we implemented a LOCO strategy for chromosome-specific testing. For variants tested on chromosome 𝑐, only variants and genes outside chromosome 𝑐 were used to construct TransMap-global phenotypes. In addition, when constructing 𝚺 DF "# , variantgene entries from the same chromosome were set to zero according to the trans definition. Each 𝒀 $ "# was standardized and used as a continuous trans-acting molecular phenotype for downstream association testing, fine-mapping and colocalization analysis.

Genome-wide trans-QTL characterization through statistical fine-mapping

Statistical fine-mapping analysis provides an LD-aware approach to pinpoint putative causal variants underlying regional association signals. Each independent signal is summarized by an 𝛼-level credible set (CS) and variantlevel posterior inclusion probabilities (PIP) 24 . TransMap defines an independent trans-QTL as a distal genetic signal represented by a 95% CS for a standardized, cell-type-resolved, donor-level trans molecular phenotype 𝒀 "# from statistical fine-mapping analysis. Each 𝒀 "# can represent an individual distal-gene expression trait (TransMap-eGene), a local WPC program score (TransMap-local), or a global sCCA program score (TransMapglobal). We summarized the resulting trans-QTL and PIP as genome-wide variant-level trans-MaxPIP annotations to evaluate their enrichment for complex-trait heritability (Methods).

Genome-wide fine-mapping is organized across 1,361 approximately independent autosomal LD blocks 26 . Each LD block is extended by 50 kb on both sides to define a fine-mapping region and reduce boundary effects for signals near block edges. For each region on chromosome 𝑐, we first assembled the corresponding trans phenotype set across three scales by excluding genes on chromosome 𝑐. We then performed fine-mapping using the SuSiE (Sum of Single Effects) model 24 with a maximum of 10 causal signals per locus and purity= 0.5. We defined a significant trans-QTL association as a 95% credible set (CS) from SuSIE containing at least one variant with a marginal association p-value below the method-specific threshold corresponding to FDR < 5%.

To assess the expected false discovery burden, we estimated the effective number of independent common variants (MAF > 5%) in the ROSMAP WGS reference panel as 619,380 (PLINK --indep-pairwise 50 1 0.2) 9 . Across ~108K individual trans-genes (average 12,444 genes, Supplementary Table 1) and ~9K trans-programs (average 1,017 programs, Supplementary Figure 1a) genome-wide scans spanning 3 cortical regions and 6 major brain cell types, we identified 91,019 and 42,030 independent 95% credible sets whose lead variant reached p-value < 5 × 10 "6 and p-value < 5 × 10 "K , respectively. Under a calibrated null, we would expect approximately 3,345 (619,380 × 108K × 5 × 10 "6 ) and 2,787 (619,380 × 9K × 5 × 10 "K ) false-positive credible sets at these thresholds, corresponding to approximate FDRs of 3.7% and 6.6% 9 . Because correlation among phenotypes does not alter the expected number of false positives, these estimates are approximately unbiased but do not account for residual p-value miscalibration, which we assess empirically using genotype-label permutations.

Genome-wide QTL discovery for curated and data-driven gene programs

To enable program-level QTL discovery beyond co-expression modules, we extended TransMap to analyze any prespecified functional gene set. For each gene set and expression context, TransMap applies the WPC procedure used for TransMap-local to derive donor-level co-regulatory activity scores. Each retained WPC is treated as a quantitative molecular phenotype and subjected to genome-wide fine-mapping across 1,361 LD blocks 26 . For trans-specific mapping of variants on chromosome 𝑐, genes located on this chromosome are excluded before phenotype construction; complementary network-wide mapping retain all member genes to capture genetic effects on the complete program. To evaluate curated biological programs, we analyzed the 50 Hallmark gene sets from the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB) previously examined using TransPCO 16 , comprising 32-200 genes and provide coherent and relatively nonredundant representation of biological states and processes. To evaluate data-driven regulatory programs, we inferred context-specific TF-target regulons separately for six major brain cell types and three bulk cortical regions using SCENIC 44 : GRNBoost2 78 was first used to estimate weighted regulatory association between human TFs and all expressed genes, after which the top highest-ranked targets per TF were partitioned according to their correlation direction and pruned using RcisTarge motif enrichment (normalized enrichment score > 3.0) 79 . The resulting motif-supported regulons and Hallmark gene sets were summarized using WPC and mapped using the same genome-wide framework. These applications establish TransMap as a general-purpose for converting curated or data-driven gene sets into quantitative phenotype for program-level QTL discovery.

Multi-phenotype colocalization of cross-cell-type cis-trans regulatory paths

A trans-QTL can represent a downstream molecular consequence of a proximal cis effect, in which local genetic regulation propagates to distal molecular phenotypes within or across cell types. These effects may further converge with downstream biomarker signals measured through proteomic, glycoproteomic and metabolomic assays. Proximal cis-regulatory genes are relatively few and typically have stronger cis-QTL effects, whereas distal trans-regulatory phenotypes are far more numerous and individually weaker 7 . This imbalance in dimensionality and association strength can substantially limit power for a single joint colocalization analysis. We therefore implemented a two-stage genome-wide multi-phenotype colocalization strategy using ColocBoost 25.

In the first stage, we identified colocalization among distal molecular phenotypes within the same 1,361 extended LD block regions. Candidate phenotypes comprised cell-type-resolved trans genes and trans programs together with trans biomarkers when available. Within each region, we retained phenotypes for which fine-mapping identified at least one 50% CS overlapping the region 26 . To reduce redundancy, highly correlated phenotypes were pruned within each phenotype class at an absolute pairwise correlation of | 𝑟 |≥ 0.7. ColocBoost was then applied jointly to the retained distal phenotypes. Each trans-only colocalization event was summarized by a 95% colocalization confidence set (CoS), variant-level variant colocalization probabilities (VCP), and a trait configuration specifying the subset of phenotypes compatible with the shared genetic signal. We retained 95% CoS as an independent locus for colocalization events when it contains at least one variant with marginal pvalue < 10 "0 for the traits in configurations.

In the second stage, we matched these distal colocalization events to events from a separate genome-wide gene-level colocalization analysis of cell-type-resolved cis-eQTL 26 . A distal trans-only colocalization event and a proximal cis-only colocalization event were integrated when their 95% CoS shared the same causal variants. Therefore, we define a `Colocalization Event` as this integrated colocalization confidence set and an associated configuration of molecular phenotypes sharing the genetic signal. Configurations that link one or more proximal cis-eGenes to one or more distal trans-eGenes or trans-ePrograms were defined as `Candidate Regulatory Configurations`, indicating the core cis-trans link and may further connect to a downstream trans-biomarker. The cis-effect cell types define 'initiating cell types', whereas the distal trans-effect cell types define 'recipient cell types' (Figure 1a). Because the two stages were connected through overlap between independently estimated colocalization events, these configurations do not represent formal joint cis-trans colocalization and cannot establish mediation or direct intercellular signaling. Nevertheless, this design allows TransMap to organize shared regulatory evidence across molecular scales and cell types for subsequent biological characterization.

AD-prioritized multi-phenotype colocalization of cis-and trans-regulatory signals

In contrast to LD-block-based genome-wide fine-mapping and colocalization analyses, AD-prioritized colocalization was organized around topologically associating domain (TAD)-based regions containing candidate AD loci. We extracted candidate AD loci curated by the FunGen-xQTL project 26 and mapped their constituent variants by genomic position to a genome-wide reference set of 1,328 TAD regions 27 . Regions containing at least one candidate AD variant were retained, and candidate variants mapping to the same TAD region were analyzed jointly. Because a TAD region may contain multiple proximal genes, each TAD region was therefore extended to encompass the cis windows of all candidate genes assigned to that region, with each window defined as ±1.5 Mb from the transcription start site 27.

For each tested TAD region on chromosome 𝑐, we performed targeted QTL mapping of all candidate molecular phenotypes at the AD variants assigned to this region. Candidate proximal phenotypes comprised cell-typesolved expression traits for genes within the TAD region; candidate distal phenotypes comprised cell-typeresolved TransMap phenotypes constructed from genes outside chromosome 𝑐. Proteomic, glycoproteomic and metabolomic phenotypes were additionally evaluated as potential downstream trans-biomarkers. A molecular phenotype was retained for colocalization analysis if at least one candidate AD variant in this TAD region showed a marginal QTL association at p-value< 10 "8 as suggested in ColocBoost 25 . We jointly analyzed all retained molecular phenotypes with an AD GWAS meta-analysis using the disease-prioritized mode of ColocBoost in each TAD region, with AD designed as the focal trait (Data resources and preprocessing below). This mode uses expedited single-effect coupling to prioritize colocalization signals involving AD while allowing multiple distinct signals within the region. Each colocalization event was summarized by a 95% CoS, where its corresponding trait configuration specified the molecular phenotypes sharing the AD-associated signal. We retained colocalization events linking AD to at least one molecular phenotype and containing at least one variant with marginal p-value < 10 "8 for AD colocalized molecular traits in configuration 25 . We then classified retained colocalization events as AD-cis, AD-trans or AD-cis-trans according to whether the configuration contained proximal cis-eGenes, distal trans phenotypes or both. AD-cis-trans configurations were interpreted as ADsupported candidate cis-trans regulatory paths. For comparison, we additionally fine-mapped the AD GWAS using SuSiE and classified an AD locus as AD-only when its 95% CS shared no variants with any AD-centered 95% CoS containing at least one molecular effect.

Empirical assessment of statistical calibration and reproducibility

To assess the calibration and robustness of TransMap, we performed two complementary empirical analyses: (i) 50:50 split-sample analyses to assess reproducibility of trans-MaxPIP annotation from genome-wide finemapping analysis, and (ii) genome-wide permutation analyses to evaluate the null calibration of fine-mapping and multi-phenotype colocalization for downstream trans-QTL discovery. These analyses evaluated two distinct properties of the framework: control of spurious discoveries under the null and generalizability of the inferred programs and genetic associations across donor subsets.

(i) Split-sample assessment of TransMap trans-MaxPIP annotation reproducibility. We randomly divided donors into two non-overlapping halves (50:50 donor-level split) for each expression profile. We ran the full workflow independently in each split, including trans phenotype construction and genome-wide fine-mapping at three trans-regulatory scales. Thus, Hotspot modules, WPC co-regulatory activity phenotypes and sCCA-derived global embeddings were estimated independently in the two splits, without transferring program definitions or model parameters between two splits. We evaluated reproducibility using two complementary metrics. First, we calculate the Pearson correlation between split-specific trans-MaxPIP annotations, separately for three transregulatory scales. Second, we evaluated whether the independently derived annotations captured consistent disease-relevance genetic information. We applied the same S-LDSC models to each split-specific trans-MaxPIP annotation and compared heritability enrichment and marginal 𝜏 * estimates (Methods below).

(ii) Permutation-based assessment of null calibration. We assessed the calibration of fine-mapping using SuSiE for individual trans genes and multi-phenotype colocalization using ColocBoost when jointly analyzing thousands of trans-eGene, trans-eProgram, and trans-biomarker phenotypes. We performed genome-wide permutations across 1,361 LD blocks used in the primary analyses. For statistical fine-mapping, we randomly shuffled donor labels in the genotype matrix while molecular phenotypes was unchanged; then we applied SuSiE to each permuted block and defined the genome-wide empirical false discovery rate (FDR) as the number of fine-mapped trans-eQTL under permutation divided by the number of trans-eQTL detected in the original data. For multiphenotype colocalization, two permutation schemes separated the effect of analyzing thousands of phenotypes from that of their observed correlation structure. First, to assess null colocalization events when cross-phenotype correlations were disrupted, we independently permuted donor labels for each trans-phenotype within each block while leaving the genotype matrix unchanged. This preserved LD among variants but disrupted genotypephenotype associations and the observed correlations among trans-phenotypes. Second, to assess null colocalization events under the phenotype covariance present in the primary analysis, we applied a single donorlabel permutation to the genotype matrix within each block while leaving all trans-phenotypes unchanged. This procedure preserved both LD among variants and covariance among trans-phenotypes while disrupting genotype-phenotype associations. We reran ColocBoost under each permutation scheme and estimated a genome-wide empirical FDR as the number of colocalization events detected under permutation divided by the number of events detected in the original data. To account for differences in the number of phenotypes tested across LD blocks, we also calculated a weighted FDR. Each detected event was weighted by the fraction of phenotype in its trait configuration among all phenotypes tested in that block, with identical weights applied to permuted and observed events. We then matched this permuted trans-only colocalization events to genome-wide cis-gene events identified from the unpermuted data. A false cis-trans match required at least one shared variant between their 95% CoS. The genome-wide empirical cis-trans FDR was calculated as the number of cistrans matches obtained under permutation divided by the number of cis-trans matches obtained in the original analysis.

Multi-omics and GWAS data sources and preprocessing

The primary empirical analyses were applied to matched whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and molecular phenotype resources from ROSMAP donors 80, 81 (average 𝑁 = 481, Supplementary Table 1). Genotype data were derived from quality-controlled WGS dosages, and molecular phenotypes were measured in the same donor cohort and matched at the donor level. The primary molecular resources included bulk and single-nucleus RNA-sequencing profiles across 6 cell types and 3 brain regions, and bulk proteomic, glycoproteomic and metabolomic measurements from the aging brain cortex. Bulk RNA-seq data were generated from postmortem tissues including dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) and anterior cingulate cortex (AC). Standard QC and adapter trimming was performed on raw reads, followed by alignment via STAR and gene expression quantification via RNASeqQC 82, 83 . Genes were removed if over 20% samples have TPM expression level of 10% or less. Single-nucleus RNA-seq data were aggregated into donor-level pseudobulk expression profiles, quantified as counts per million (CPM), for major brain cell classes, including excitatory neurons (Exc), inhibitory neurons (Inh), microglia (Mic), astrocytes (Ast), oligodendrocytes (Oli) and oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPC). For downstream biomarkers, Selected Reaction Monitoring (SRM) proteomics was performed on DLPFC samples, and the peptide relative abundances were log2 transformed after quality control and filtering for proteins quantified in at lease 50% of samples. Glycoproteome was also perform on DLPFC samples using an improved glycopeptide-enrichment workflow followed by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry 84 . The 9,044 detected glycopetiforms originated from 1,217 distinct glycoproteins, which are log-transformed after excluding glycopeptiforms with fewer than two-thirds samples with valid measurements. Missing values for protein and glycoprotein were imputed using the grouped Empirical Bayesian Matrix Factorization method 85 . The 656 brain metabolites were measured in DLPFC samples and profiled using untargeted mass spectrometry, where metabolite abundances were log-transformed 86 . For all trans-acting molecular phenotypes, we removed the technical factors (batch, RNA integrity number, post-mortem interval), biological covariates (sex, age at death), and the top 15 genotype PC 26 . Details on the consideration of additional hidden factor derived from phenotype matrix were described in Supplementary Note S1. We restricted the QTL analysis to autosomal variants with minor allele frequency (MAF) > 0.05 and minor allele count (MAC) > 5.

For AD-centered TransMap analysis, we constructed a custom LD reference panel from the Alzheimer's Disease Sequencing Project (ADSP), consisting of approximately 17,000 whole-genome sequenced (WGS) individuals of European ancestry. We primarily used a recent AD GWAS meta-analysis summary statistics (cases=128,681, controls=849,833) 54 after performing quality control against this reference panel, including allele harmonization and LD mismatch detection using SLALOM, with flagged suspicious variants removed 87 . As a secondary AD GWAS, we considered meta-analysis summary statistics with a smaller effective sample size (cases=111,326, controls=677,663) 56 used in our previous analysis 25 , followed by the same allele harmonization and quality control steps above.

Benchmarks of local program trans-regulatory analysis

For TransMap-local, we benchmarked two complementary components: the regulatory coherence of local coexpression modules and its utility for trans-QTL mapping. First, using independent empirical trans-eQTL datasets, we tested whether the co-expression modules defining local programs grouped genes with coordinated trans-regulatory effects. We used empirical evidence because simulations do not readily capture the complex covariance structure of gene expression in human tissues. Second, we used simulations to assess whether WPC-based program phenotypes improved trans-QTL detection for a specified local program.

We first benchmarked Hotspot against WGCNA, a widely used method for detecting co-expression modules, using external and internal trans-eQTL resources. Hotspot and WGCNA modules were constructed from the same donor-level expression resource, with method-specific parameters described in Methods. Variant-program pairs were considered active when the program-level association passed the Bonferroni-corrected threshold of 10 "0 . For an active pair between variant 𝑗 and module 𝒢 = , trans-eQTL coherence was defined as where, 𝑝 M!

NOPO denotes the individual-gene trans-eQTL p-value for variant 𝑗 and gene 𝑔 in module 𝒢 = . Larger coherence indicates that a program-level association is supported by multiple genes in the module rather than by a single outlier gene. We implemented a match internal benchmark evaluated ROSMAP cell-type-resolved co-expression modules using matched ROSMAP trans-eQTL association, In addition to ROSMAP benchmark, we also used two external resources to benchmark program-level coherence for co-expression module detection methods. For blood-based benchmarking, GTEx whole-blood expression profiles (𝑁 = 673) 7 were paired with eQTLGen trans-eQTL associations for 10,317 tested trait-associated variants 4 , with 3,961 independent variants after LD pruning (𝑟 7 < 0.1) used in the program-level coherence evaluation. For brain-based benchmarking, GTEx brain cortex expression profiles (𝑁 = 208) 7 were paired with MetaBrain trans-eQTL associations for 228,819 tested variants 10 , with 25,035 independent variants after LD pruning (𝑟 7 < 0.1) used for the same evaluation.

We next evaluated program-level trans-QTL testing for a specified gene program containing 𝑀 genes using simulation studies. We first considered a single variant affecting the gene program through a cis-regulated gene. Let 𝑮 ∈ ℝ ,×2 denote the genotype vector for the tested variant, sampled from Binomial(2, 𝑓), where 𝑓 was drawn from the empirical MAF distribution in ROSMAP donors (Supplementary Figure S2a). Let 𝛽 +QR denote the effect size from the variant to the cis-gene, and let 𝜷 +QR"STUPR = (𝛽 =,+QR"STUPR ) =>2 ?

denote the vector of effects from the cis-gene to the 𝑀 trans-genes. We generated expression for the cis-gene, 𝒀 +QR , and each trans-gene, 𝒀 =,STUPR , as where 𝜀 ∼ 𝒩(0, 𝐼 , ) denotes residual noise for the cis-gene.

The residual expression matrix 𝑬 = [𝑬 2 , … , 𝑬 ? ] was generated with row-wise covariance 𝚺 F , using an AR(1) structure (𝚺 F ) M$ = 𝜌 |M"$| . We assigned 𝛽 +QR such that the per-SNP cis heritability of 0.04 and varied 𝛽 =,+QR"STUPR to control the per-SNP cis to trans heritability 25, 39 , defined as per-SNP trans heritability = 2𝑓(1 -𝑓)(𝛽 +QR 𝛽 +QR"STUPR ) 7.

The primary numerical study considered six broad settings: (i) program size (𝑀 = 20,50,100), matched to the median size of modules in real data analyses; (ii) sample size, varied from 400 to 1,000; (iii) the proportion of causal trans-genes affected by the variant, varied from 0% to 100%, with 0% used to evaluate type-I error (T1E); (iv) residual expression correlation structure 𝚺 F , with 𝜌 = 0.1,0.3,0.5 ; (v) per-SNP trans heritability values corresponding to low-(0.0025), intermediate-(0.004) and high-power (0.01) regimes 39 ; and (vi) sign heterogeneity of trans-QTL effects, where homogeneous effects assign all causal trans-effects positive signs and heterogeneous effects assign balanced positive and negative signs. In each replicate, we randomly sampled 1-3 independent causal variants with probabilities of 85.9%, 10.6% and 3.6%, respectively, based on their observed frequencies on ROSMAP (Figure 2b). When multiple variants were simulated, each variant affected a disjoint subset of genes within the same module. TransMap-local, with Bonferroni correction across retained WPCs (𝜆 > 1), was compared with standard single-gene trans-eQTL testing using Bonferroni correction across genes in the module, Eigengene testing using only the first expression PC in a program 40 , and TransPCO, an omnibus test that combines multiple PC-based association tests 16 . Details of each competing method are described in Methods. Performance was evaluated at the level of trans-QTL discovery using a significance threshold of p-value < 10 "0 . We used two principal metrics: statistical power and T1E. Power was defined as the proportion of true module-level trans-QTL correctly identified across replicates, and T1E was defined as the proportion of null replicates in which a trans-QTL was detected. For each simulation setting, 1,000 replicates were generated to evaluate statistical power and 10 6 replicates were generated to evaluate T1E at nominal pvalue of 10 "0.

Benchmarks of global program trans-regulatory analysis

For TransMap-global, we benchmarked whether sparse association-driven embeddings recovered the underlying variant-gene trans-effect structure. Unlike the local benchmark, which evaluates trans-QTL detection for a specified gene module, the global benchmark evaluates recovery of low-dimensional regulatory structure at the variant-gene pair level. We used a structured causal-network simulation following the benchmark developed for ARCHIE 17 , in which groups of variants act through upstream regulated genes and induce coordinated but indirect distal expression responses. The simulation contains 40 trans-active causal variants and nine distal genes, with 20 additional non-trans variants included to evaluate false discovery rate (FDR). In this structured network, trans-active variants are organized into five-SNP blocks, and each block affects the expression of one proximal cis-gene mediator. The proximal mediators then propagate effects through three downstream trans-gene layers (Figure 1f). Same as in local-program simulation, genotype vectors were simulated independently for 60 variants. For each variant 𝑗, 𝑮 M ∼ Binomial(2, 𝑓 M ), where 𝑓 M was drawn from the empirical MAF distribution in ROSMAP donors (Supplementary Figure S2a). Let 𝛽 ℓ denote the effect size in layer ℓ , for ℓ = 1,2,3 , where ℓ = 1 represents the propagation from cis-gene mediators to the first layer of trans-genes. Let 𝒀 ℓ denote expression of trans-genes in layer ℓ. The layered graph can be summarized schematically as where 𝜺 ℓ ∼ 𝒩(0, 𝐼 , ) denotes residual noise for gene expression.

We assigned 𝛽 * such that the per-SNP cis heritability of 0.04 and varied 𝛽 ℓ to control the path-level trans heritability for different causal layers, defined as 2𝑓(1 -𝑓) ∏ 𝛽 W 7 ℓ W>* for a representative path at layer ℓ = 1,2,3.

The primary numerical study considered four broad settings: (i) trans heritability, varied by changing the downstream layer-specific effect sizes to span low-(0.0025), intermediate-(0.004) and high-power (0.01) regimes for the weakest layer, and (ii) embedding sparsity, varied by changing the target proportion of non-zero loadings under sparse (0.4), dense (0.8) and cross-validation-optimized settings. We additionally generated an independent held-out sample of 1,000 individuals for methods requiring an expression covariance estimate.
